Hibernation and aestivation: Frogs are poikilothermic or cold blooded animals and their body temperature changes according to the temperature of surrounding environment. Their body temperature may fall abruptly in winters which may threaten life. To protect from such a harsh situation, they remain hidden or dormant inside the moist burrow or under soft damp bottom mud. This phenomenon is called hibernation or ‘winter sleep’. This duration lasts for about 3 months. At the time of hibernation, nostrils and mouth remain closed and stops feeding, excretion, become metabolically inactive, breathe only by cutaneous respiration and survive on reserve food such as glycogen and fat stored in their body. During summer also, they remain inactive or become dormant under the mud to escape from extreme high temperature of the environment, which is called aestivation. Aestivation lasts for about 15 days. During this period, they occasionally come out in search of food. Aestivation is commonly called summer sleep. iv. Croaking: It is the characteristic sound produced by male frogs during breeding season, also called sex call or mating call. It is heard louder and produced only by male frogs to attract female frogs for mating purpose. Males have a pair of bluish skin patches or folds on the throat region, called vocal sacs which are used to croak.

v. Breeding Rainy season (July to September) is breeding season for frog in which males gather in shallow water and start producing croaking sound to attract female frog. While mating, male mounts on the back of female and grasps the female firmly with the help of nuptial pad or copulatory pad developed on its first or index finger of fore limbs. This sexual embrace is also called false copulation or amplexus. Hence, there is no true copulation or mating in frogs. Meanwhile, female frog gets stimulated and starts laying eggs in water through cloaca. Mass of eggs intermingled with gelatin like material on the water surface is called spawn. Male discharges seminal fluid or milt containing sperms over the cluster of eggs or spawn. Thus, fertilization is external, taking place in water, which in turn forms zygotes. Then, zygotes develop into free swimming and completely aquatic tadpole within about 15 days. Tadpole after few weeks gets metamorphosed into amphibious adult.
Figure 8.4.4 A male frog croaking by inflating vocal sacs vi. Camouflage:

Frogs can change their body colour according to the surrounding where they are living so that they are not easily noticed by enemies. This is called camouflage. Change in colour occurs due to the dispersion of amoeboid pigmented cells called chromotophores found in dermis of skin. vii. Ways of protection from enemies Enemies of frog are snakes, human beings, birds such as crane, hawk, eagle, crow etc. Similarly, small frogs are also eaten up by larger frog. Human beings also kill large number of frogs for dissection in laboratory to study their anatomy. Ways adopted by frogs to protect themselves from enemies are: a. They can change its body colour according to the surrounding so that enemies can’t detect it easily. b. Frog suddenly ejects urine, when tried to catch. c. They have slippery skin because of the presence of mucous glands due to which they can’t be easily caught by enemies. d. They have habit of living near fresh water sources and quickly dive into the water on arrival of enemies.

Shape, size and colour: Body of adult frog is somewhat spindle shaped which is pointed anteriorly and rounded at the posterior side. It has dorso-ventrally flattened and bilaterally symmetrical body (body can be divided into similar halves by a single plane). The size of a fully-grown adult is about 18cm length and 8 cm width. Skin is thin, moist, slimy and smooth without any hard scales or exoskeleton. Skin of frog is slippery because of the presence of mucus gland. Frog never drinks water but absorb it through skin. Moist skin also serves as respiratory surface in frog. Dorsal side of frog is green colored with black or brown spots but its ventral surface is pale yellow or Biology, Grade 11 | 387
whitish coloured. A light yellow or white coloured thick line runs mid-dorsally from the tip of snout to the cloacal opening at the back.
